content.text: Mentorship and practice develop skills and connect individuals to the community and heritage.
Through practice and mentorship, people turn skill into voice and work into art.
In Lesson 41, students revise and publish their explanatory essays and process documents. In Lesson 42, students present their work during a Gallery of Learning activity.

Reviewing Process Writing
Directions:
Briefly review what you learned about process writing and process documents earlier in the unit. Then, read the sample process document.
How to Make Pottery
Prepare the Clay:
First, the clay is gathered and purified by mixing it with water and then draining it through sieves one or more times.

attrs.alt: A potter pours liquid clay from a large vase through a sieve resting on top of a bucket.
attrs.bestCaption: A potter refines the clay by mixing it with water and pouring it through a sieve. Photo by: Maskot / Contributor

content.text: Shape the Clay:
Second, the clay is sculpted using simple tools or a pottery wheel. The minerals in the clay allow it to hold its shape.

attrs.alt: Image of two hands shaping a bowl on a pottery wheel. One hand is positioned inside the bowl, the other is at its base holding a small sponge.
attrs.bestCaption: A potter shapes the clay on a pottery wheel. Photo by: sestovic / Contributor

content.text: Dry and Fire the Clay:
Next, the clay is left out to dry before being fired in the kiln to drive off any remaining moisture.

attrs.alt: Image of a clay teapot and two small clay pots sitting on a shelf.
attrs.bestCaption: Clay pottery air-dries before going into the kiln. Photo by: Johannes Geyer / Contributor

content.text: Glaze the Pottery:
Lastly, the fired pottery is covered with different glazes containing metal oxides that create different colors once the pottery is fired again in an electric, soda, or raku kiln.

attrs.alt: Image of a potter at a pottery wheel painting blue glaze onto a bowl.
attrs.bestCaption: After pottery comes out of the kiln, it is covered in different glazes before being fired a second time. Photo by: Alex Potemkin / Contributor

content.text: Directions:
Review the model process document and notice what makes it successful.
What do you notice about this process document?
Successful process documents:
are written for a specific audience;
use clear, concise language;
use temporal connectors to show the sequence of the steps;
are organized in a way that is easy to follow; and
often include images or illustrations that show each step.
Reflection
Routine: Reflection | Domain: CFU | Action: Likert Scale + Write-on Lines}
Reflect on your understanding of the qualities of a successful process document using the Reflection routine.
How confident do you feel about your ability to develop a successful process document of your own?
Then write a sentence explaining how you can better understand this skill.
Drafting a Process Document
Directions:
You will create a process document that shows the steps of learning or making a craft, such as pottery, weaving, or another art form.
Now that you’ve drafted your explanatory essays, the next step is to create a process document. Part 2 of the Performance Task asks you to do one of two things:
Make a process document that shows the steps of
learning
a craft.
Make a process document that shows the steps of
making
a craft.
As a class, generate a list of crafts and trades to use for your process document.
What are some examples of crafts and trades we have learned about during the unit?
What are some other crafts and trades you are familiar with?
Share your responses, then begin creating your process document.

Select a craft or trade. Then, create a process document that shows the steps of learning or making that craft. Your classmates are the target audience for your process document; this means it should be written in a way that someone your age will understand. Your process document should:
Include a title
Include at least four steps
Include at least two relevant images or illustrations with captions
Have a clear organizational structure
Use clear, concise writing
Use temporal connectors
Draft your process document, writing each step clearly in order using temporal connectors, and check for correct capitalization, punctuation, and spelling as you go.
You will have 30 minutes to begin drafting your process document. Focus on getting your steps written clearly in order with temporal connectors.
Temporal connectors are transition words and phrases that show the order or sequence of events or steps. They tell the reader
when
things happen in relation to each other. Common examples include
first
second
third
next
then
after
before
meanwhile
finally
subsequently
at the same time
once
later
, and
eventually
If you don’t finish, you’ll continue working on it for homework and revise later. Quality matters more than completion today.
Before you move on from each step, check for correct capitalization, punctuation, and spelling of key terms. Your captions should look as polished as the ones in our model.
Checklist
You will turn in your process description for feedback. A strong draft should:
☐ Select a craft or art form to describe.
☐ Identify at least four steps in a process.
☐ Use temporal connectors to describe steps in a process.
☐ Include at least two cause–effect connectors that explain why a step matters.
☐ Use clear and concise writing.
☐ Include relevant details and images with captions that reference specific steps in their process documents.

Connection to Today’s Learning

Today, you will begin working on Part 2 of the Showcase Performance Task: creating a process document that shows the steps of learning or making a craft.

Reviewing Process Writing
Briefly review with students what they learned about process writing and process documents earlier in Unit 2.

A Single Shard
and in the article “Cracking the Science Behind Pottery with MudFire Pottery Studio.”

content.text: Say:
This process document is based on the simple step-by-step process we co-constructed in Lesson 8.
Ask:
What do you notice about this process document?
It includes a title. It uses numbers/headers to show the steps. It uses temporal connectors. It includes illustrations with captions to show each step.
Say:
Successful process documents:
Are written for a specific audience;
Use clear, concise language;
Use temporal connectors to show the sequence of the steps;
Are organized in a way that is easy to follow; and
Often include images or illustrations that show each step.
Say:
Use these features as a checklist as you begin drafting your own process document today.
If time permits, find other examples from the Internet of process documents to share with students. Discuss whether each process document is successful using the above criteria.
Help students recognize the language and structure features that make process writing clear: sequential steps, cause–effect links, and visuals that “do work” by clarifying what the text describes.
Validate students’ funds of knowledge: cooking, sports, hairstyling, repairing bikes, family traditions—any familiar process can become a strong model for clear process writing.
Name the 3 required clarity features explicitly:
Sequence (first, next, then, finally).
Cause–effect (because, so, as a result).
Visual-to-text links (caption + “This image shows . . .”).
Model “caption discipline”: caption tells what step, alt text tells what is visible, and the sentence in the step explains why it matters.
Require students to identify the audience and check readability: “Would a classmate understand this without you explaining it?”
“First, ___ so that ___.”
“Next, ___ because ___.”
“After that, ___; as a result, ___.”
“This image supports step __ by showing ___.”
Revoice vague steps into action verbs: “Do the clay” → “Gather and purify the clay by mixing it with water and pouring it through sieves.”
Press for cause–effect precision: “Dry it” → “Dry it so moisture evaporates; otherwise, the piece can crack in the kiln.”
Clarify visual links: “Insert picture here” → “This image shows step 2 because it captures ___.”
If steps are out of order → Prompt: “Number the steps 1–4, and add a temporal connector to each.”
If the writing is list-like but unclear → Prompt: “Add one ‘why’ sentence using because/so for steps 2 and 3.”
If visuals feel decorative → Prompt: “Write a caption that names the step + one detail the image clarifies.”
Students can point to at least 4 steps, each with a temporal connector.
Students include at least 2 cause–effect connectors that explain why a step matters.
Students explain how a caption/visual clarifies the step (not just “it looks cool”).
Reflection
Reflect on your understanding of the qualities of a successful process document using the Reflection routine.
How confident do you feel about your ability develop a successful process document of your own?
Then write a sentence explaining how you can better understand this skill.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Temporal connectors

Review the use of temporal connectors to show chronological or sequential order. Display a bank of temporal connectors that students can use when drafting their process documents. Ex. first, second, third, then, next, after, before, finally.
Struggling with: Selecting transitional words and phrases

Provide students with brief prompts to help them determine which transitional words and phrases are appropriate to use and when. Ex. “What type of relationship are you trying to show?” “Do these ideas show cause or effect/examples/time order?” “Does this sentence/paragraph build on ideas from the writing that came before it?”
Ready for extension: Using transitional words and phrases
Challenge students to use other transitional words and phrases to make other connections throughout their process documents, including cause–effect relationships.
Connection to Today’s Learning
Say:
Today, you will apply what you know about writing about processes to draft your own process document about learning or making a craft.
Students will revisit how to write a process document and evaluate what makes a process document successful.
Learning in Action: Drafting a Process Document
(30 minutes)
Display Part 2 of the Showcase Performance Task:
Say these Directions:

This process document is Part 2 of your Performance Task and should clearly show either how to learn or how to make a craft. You will create a process document that shows the steps of learning or making a craft, such as pottery, weaving, or another art form.
Say:
Now that you’ve drafted your explanatory essays, the next step is to create a process document. Part 2 of the Performance Task asks you to do one of two things:
Make a process document that shows the steps of
learning
a craft.
Make a process document that shows the steps of
making
a craft.
Teacher Tip
Briefly discuss the differences between
learning
and
making

, noting how the steps to learn a craft will likely reflect the stages of learning, while the steps of making a craft will more closely reflect the process document students created as a class about the pottery process.
As a class, generate a list of crafts and trades that students can use for their process documents.
Ask:
What are some examples of crafts and trades we have learned about during the unit?
Pottery, Ndebele mural painting, kintsugi, basketry, Zuni pottery, sculpting, weaving, boot making, clog making, leatherworking, globe making
Ask:
What are some other crafts and trades you are familiar with?
Weaving, knitting, beading, ironworking
Record student responses on the board. Then transition students to creating their process documents.
Say:

Select a craft or trade. Then create a process document that shows the steps of learning or making that craft. Your classmates are the target audience for your process document; this means it should be written in a way that someone your age will understand. Your process document should:
Include a title
Include at least four steps
Include at least two relevant images or illustrations with captions
Have a clear organizational structure
Use clear, concise writing
Use temporal connectors
Teacher Tip

Generating a list as a class ensures all students have viable topic options and activates shared knowledge from the unit. Distinguishing between “steps to learn a craft” and “steps to make a craft” prevents students from conflating the two structures—
learning
processes follow stages (observe → try → fail → refine → create), and
making
processes follow sequential production steps (e.g., gather → shape → fire → glaze).
Say:
You will have 30 minutes to begin drafting your process document. Focus on getting your steps written clearly in order with temporal connectors.
Say:
Temporal connectors are transition words and phrases that show the order or sequence of events or steps. They tell the reader
when
things happen in relation to each other. Common examples include
first
second
third
next
then
after
before
meanwhile
finally
subsequently
at the same time
once
later
, and
eventually
Say:
Use the checklist to make sure your process document meets all requirements before moving on.
Say:
If you don’t finish, you’ll continue with homework and revise in Lesson 35. Quality matters more than completion today.
Say:
Before you move on from each step, check for correct capitalization, punctuation, and spelling of key terms. Your captions should look as polished as the ones in our model.
Have students work independently to draft their process documents. Students may use the Flowchart graphic organizer to write down and organize their ideas.
Teacher Tip

Students often write a bare numbered list (“Step 1: Get clay. Step 2: Shape it”) without explaining why each step matters or how it connects to the next. Circulate during drafting and prompt, “You’ve told me
what
to do—now tell me
why
this step matters or what happens if I skip it.”

Support students in drafting a complete process document (title + 4+ steps + 2+ visuals) that is cohesive and easy to follow, using sequential language, cause–effect connectors, and explicit text-to-visual references.
Encourage culturally relevant processes (family recipes, community crafts, local trades) while keeping the document readable and school-appropriate for peers.
Require a process choice up front:
Model one “tight” step and one “expanded” step so students see how to control length for clarity.
During drafting, pause once for a quick checklist: “Do I have sequence + cause–effect + visual link?”
Clarify audience: replace jargon with a quick appositive: “kiln (a very hot oven for pottery).”
“In step __, the goal is to ___. This matters because ___.”
“If ___ happens, then ___; therefore, the maker should ___.”
“This photo/illustration shows ___, which helps the reader understand ___.”
“Finally, the process ends when ___.”
Making a craft (materials/tools → steps → product), OR
Learning a craft (stages of learning → practice loop → mastery/creating).
Require students to write each step in this mini-structure: step label + action → why (cause–effect) → visual link (caption reference).
Upgrade sequence words: and then → next, afterward, meanwhile, finally.
Strengthen cause–effect: “This helps” → “This prevents ___” / “This allows ___” / “As a result, ___.”
If steps are missing cause–effect → Prompt: “Add one sentence to steps 2 and 3 starting with because or so.”
If the document is hard to follow → Prompt: “Add sub-bullets for tools/materials under step 1, and shorten step 4 to one clear action.”
If visuals aren’t connected → Prompt: “Add a caption that begins ‘Step __:’ and one sentence in the step that says, ‘This image shows . . .’”
Titles are specific and match the process (learn vs. make).
Students include at least 4 steps with clear temporal connectors.
Students include at least 2 visuals with captions that name the step.
Students use at least 2 cause–effect connectors explaining why steps matter.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Describing the steps to make a craft
Review the various crafts and art forms students have learned about throughout the unit. Re-share relevant articles and videos as needed to help students identify steps in the process.
Struggling with: Describing the steps to learn a craft

Provide students with brief prompts to help them identify steps in the process of learning a craft. Ex. “Who might you talk to in order to learn a new craft?” “What resources might tell you how to learn a craft?” “How do the stages of learning—observing, trying, failing, refining, and creating—connect to learning a craft?”
Ready for extension: Creating a process document
Challenge students to create a process document for a topic that is unique or special to them. Invite students to share their process documents in small groups or with the class.
Checklist
You will turn in your process description for feedback. A strong draft should:
☐ Select a craft or art form to describe.
☐ Identify at least four steps in a process.
☐ Use temporal connectors to describe steps in a process.
☐ Include at least two cause–effect connectors that explain why a step matters.
☐ Use clear and concise writing.
☐ Include relevant details and images with captions that reference specific steps in their process documents.
Learning in Action: Drafting a Process Document
Students will draft a process document explaining how to make or learn a craft or art form.
3–2–1 Summary
Say these Directions:
Work in small groups of three or four to co-construct a 3–2–1 Summary about process documents. Remember to include:
3 important words or phrases
2 key details or ideas
1 sentence explaining the purpose of a process document
3 Important Words or Phrases
2 Key Ideas or Details
1 Gist Sentence
step-by-step
clear and concise
organized
Process documents show the order in which steps or actions happen using temporal connectors.
Successful process documents use clear language for a specific audience.
Process documents are step-by-step descriptions that explain how or why something is done.
Exit Check Self-Assessment:
Review your process document draft, and address the following prompts:
How many steps did you include? (Target: 4+)
Highlight or underline two temporal connectors you used.
Star one cause–effect sentence that explains
why
a step matters.
Do your visuals/captions connect to specific steps? (yes / not yet)
Turn in your draft with this self-assessment attached.
Students will co-construct a 3–2–1 Summary to review what they have learned about process documents and process writing.

Instruct students to continue drafting their explanatory essays and process documents in their Journal. Students should focus on completing their process document, ensuring that it includes clear steps, relevant visuals with captions, and explanations of why each step matters.

standards.description: Introduce a topic or thesis statement; organize ideas, concepts, and information, using strategies such as definition, classification, comparison/contrast, and cause/effect; include formatting (e.g., headings), graphics (e.g., charts, tables), and multimedia when useful to aiding comprehension.
Use precise language and domain-specific vocabulary to inform about or explain the topic.
Develop the topic with relevant facts, definitions, concrete details, quotations, or other information and examples.
Use appropriate transitions to clarify the relationships among ideas and concepts.
Use punctuation (commas, parentheses, dashes) to set off nonrestrictive/parenthetical elements.

Write routinely over extended time frames (time for research, reflection, and revision) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of discipline-specific tasks, purposes, and audiences.
Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.
Write clear and coherent summaries of texts and experiences using complete and concise sentences and key words (e.g., from notes or graphic organizers).
Write brief summaries of texts and experiences using complete sentences and key words (e.g., from notes or graphic organizers).
Write increasingly concise summaries of texts and experiences using complete sentences and key words (e.g., from notes or graphic organizers).

Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations using appropriate register (e.g., to reflect on multiple perspectives) using a variety of learned phrases, indirect reported speech (e.g., I heard you say X, and Gabriel just pointed out Y), as well as open responses.

Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations (e.g., to gain and hold the floor or ask for clarification) using basic learned phrases (e.g., I think..., Would you please repeat that?), as well as open responses.
Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations (e.g., to provide counterarguments) using an expanded set of learned phrases (I agree with X, but...), as well as open responses.

Combine clauses in a wide variety of ways (e.g., creating compound and complex sentences) to make connections between and join ideas, for example, to express a reason (e.g., He stayed at home on Sunday to study for Monday’s exam), to make a concession (e.g., She studied all night even though she wasn’t feeling well), or to link two ideas that happen at the same time (e.g., The students worked in groups while their teacher walked around the room).
Combine clauses in a few basic ways to make connections between and join ideas (e.g., creating compound sentences using and, but, so).

Combine clauses in an increasing variety of ways (e.g., creating compound and complex sentences) to make connections between and join ideas, for example, to express a reason (e.g., He stayed at home on Sunday to study for Monday’s exam) or to make a concession (e.g., She studied all night even though she wasn’t feeling well).
